contentBlocks.text: This week you've explored negative numbers three ways. Today: apply all of it to a real comparison problem!

Real problem: three cities recorded these overnight low temperatures: City A was -8°F, City B was 3°F, and City C was -15°F. Which city was coldest? Which was warmest? Remember: on a number line, further left (more negative) means colder/smaller, even though -15 might look like a 'bigger' number than -8.
You just solved a real comparison problem using negative numbers! Tomorrow we'll review everything from this week.

objectives: Compare a mixed set of positive and negative numbers in a real-world context
Correctly identify the coldest and warmest temperatures from the three-city example
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review this week's number-line and absolute-value work.
2. Model the three-city temperature comparison.
3. Have the child identify the coldest and warmest cities.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's cumulative review.
differentiationTips: Struggling: place all three temperatures on a number line together before comparing
Ready for more: ask the child to add a fourth city's temperature and re-rank all four
This is the week's synthesis moment — applying number-line ordering to a genuine real-world comparison problem
teacherGuide.answerKey: City C (-15°F) was coldest. City B (3°F) was warmest.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses Common Core Grade 6 standard 6.NS.7b: writing, interpreting, and explaining statements of order for rational numbers in real-world contexts.

generationData.instructions: Use the three temperatures (City A: -8°F, City B: 3°F, City C: -15°F) to answer each question.

rows.problem: Order all three temperatures from coldest to warmest.
